opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing is that you have to be comfortable living with two timelines at once. Autonomous driving is a field where the long-term vision is very clear: eventually the car drives itself, safely, everywhere. But the path there is full of near-term pressure: you need to ship something, satisfy customers, keep the team motivated, and survive financially. A good leader can hold both without letting one swallow the other. If you only chase the grand vision, you burn out the company before you get there. If you only chase quarterly deliverables, you end up building something that's a dead end technically.

The second thing is technical judgment. This industry has gone through several paradigm shifts in a short time: from rule-based systems to modular deep learning, then toward end-to-end models, and now people are talking about world models and large-scale foundation models for driving. At each of these turning points, the leader has to decide when to bet on the new approach and when to stick with what works. That's not something you can fully delegate. You don't have to write the code yourself, but you have to understand the problem deeply enough to know when the data is telling you something important and when it's just noise.

Third, and maybe most underrated, is respect for safety and for reality. In a lot of tech fields, you can move fast, break things, and patch them later. In driving, a mistake can cost someone's life. So the leader needs to build a culture where people feel safe raising problems, where the long-tail cases are taken seriously, and where nobody is incentivized to hide a failure just to hit a demo deadline. That honesty, internally and externally, matters a lot. The industry has had periods of overpromising, and that erodes trust for everyone.

And finally, I'd say patience combined with urgency. It sounds contradictory, but it's the reality. Progress in this field often comes in steps: long plateaus, then sudden jumps. A leader has to keep the team focused and resourced through the plateaus, and then move very fast when the breakthrough comes. The people who succeed are the ones who are still at the table when the technology finally clicks.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think people often assume leadership in autonomous driving is about technical vision, and that matters, but I'd actually put it third.

The first thing is being able to hold a very long time horizon while making very short-term decisions. This industry has been "two years away" for over a decade. A leader has to genuinely believe in the destination, otherwise the team senses it and the best people leave. But at the same time, you have to make honest quarterly calls about what you can ship, what sensors you can afford, which cities you enter. If you only have the long vision, you burn money and lose credibility. If you only have the short-term discipline, you end up building a driver-assist feature and calling it autonomy.

The second thing is an almost obsessive relationship with truth. In most software, if you overstate your progress, you miss a deadline. Here, if you overstate your disengagement numbers or your long-tail coverage, someone can get hurt, and the whole industry pays for it. So an effective leader builds an organization where bad news travels fast. Engineers need to feel safer reporting a scary edge case than hiding it. I've seen companies where the metrics dashboards look beautiful and nobody wants to drive in the car. That's a leadership failure, not an engineering one.

Then third, yes, technical judgment. Not that the leader has to write the perception code, but they have to understand the tradeoffs deeply enough to resist bad consensus. Vision-only versus lidar, end-to-end versus modular, when to rely on maps. The answers shift as the data shifts, and the leader has to know when the team is defending a past decision versus defending the right one.

And underneath all of it, I'd say humility with regulators and the public. We are asking cities to trust a machine with their streets. The leaders who treat that as a negotiation to win tend to lose. The ones who treat it as a relationship to earn tend to be the ones still operating five years later.

astra-6.text:
I think an effective leader in autonomous driving needs technical judgment, humility, and a strong sense of responsibility. You need to understand the technology well enough to ask hard questions, but also recognize where your own knowledge—and the system’s capabilities—end.

A big part of the job is creating an environment where people can bring you bad news early. If an engineer finds a failure case, you want the team to examine it, not explain it away. Safety has to influence what you measure, what you prioritize, and when you decide something is ready.

You also need to bring different disciplines together. Research, engineering, vehicle operations, and product teams may see the same problem differently. A good leader helps them work toward a clear goal while keeping those different perspectives in the conversation. For me, the test is whether the team can make steady progress and stay honest about what still doesn’t work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think an effective leader in autonomous driving needs technical judgment, humility, and a strong sense of responsibility. You need to understand the technology well enough to ask hard questions, but also recognize where your own knowledge ends and listen to the people closest to the problem.

The real test is how you make decisions under uncertainty. When a team shows progress, can you distinguish a convincing demonstration from evidence that the system is ready for real roads? Can people raise safety concerns without feeling they’re slowing everyone down?

You also need to give people a clear direction. Bring research, engineering, and operations together around measurable goals, and make sure everyone understands what evidence is needed before taking the next step. For me, leadership means helping a team move forward while staying honest about what it hasn’t solved yet.
